idiom_name: @TaskLocal task-scoped values, actor isolation, @MainActor; Thread.threadDictionary for legacy interop
implementation_notes: Swift deliberately moves away from threads: `@TaskLocal` values are bound with `$name.withValue(...)` for a scope, inherited by child tasks, and cannot outlive the task (SE-0311 frames them as the structured replacement for thread-local/queue-specific values, whose 'set and forget' lifetime causes leaks and unexpected reads); actor isolation and `@MainActor` let the compiler require that mutable state is touched by one actor at a time, including main-thread-confined UI state. Thread-based mechanisms still exist for interop - `Thread.current.threadDictionary` from Foundation - but a serial DispatchQueue or an actor is preferred, because tasks hop between threads between suspension points and thread identity is explicitly not guaranteed. Keep the classic thread-local form only for APIs that demand thread affinity (C libraries using TLS, pre-concurrency frameworks).
pitfalls: @TaskLocal is read-only: values can only be bound in a scope, never set - mutation needs another mechanism, and detached tasks do not inherit bindings at all.
Actor isolation is not thread confinement: an actor may resume on different threads, so wrapping a thread-affine C library needs a custom executor or explicit locking.
Thread.threadDictionary does not follow tasks; under async/await the value disappears or reappears on another thread across suspension points (the documented motivation for SE-0311).
